title: Ex 3.8 #5 · Grabbing 15 balls when there's one white ball
prompt: A bag holds 20 red balls, 20 blue balls and 20 green balls (balls of the same color are identical), plus a single white ball. You reach in and grab 15 balls. How many different outcomes are possible?
answer_format: A whole number, or an expression for it like 26^4 or binom(10, 3).

mistakes.hint: That treats white like the other colors, as if you could grab several white balls. There is only one.
That counts only the grabs without the white ball.
When the white ball is in your hand, only 14 of the grabbed balls are red, blue or green.

hints: Split into two cases: the white ball is in your grab, or it isn't.
In each case the rest of the grab is a multiset of red, blue and green balls, which stars and bars counts. You take at most 15 of these, so the limit of 20 per color never matters.
solution: Without the white ball, the grab is a 15-element multiset of red, blue and green: 15 stars and 2 bars, so $\binom{17}{15} = 136$ outcomes.
With the white ball, the other 14 balls form a multiset of red, blue and green: $\binom{16}{14} = 120$ outcomes.
By the addition principle there are $136 + 120 = 256$ outcomes.

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses multisets and stars and bars (Section 3.8) with the addition principle.
